claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys is primarily governed by kinetically slowed atomic diffusion rather than configurational entropy alone.
The slowed diffusion is caused by a high density of nanoscale grain boundaries.
The proposed starting materials are equimolar, single-phase solid solutions with nanoscale grains.
Nanoscale grains produce a high grain-boundary density.
A controlled grain-size comparison can distinguish the proposed grain-boundary mechanism from alternatives.
High thermal energy between 600°C and 1200°C would normally promote phase transformations, segregation, or oxidation.
Grain boundaries act as kinetic barriers that limit atomic diffusion across interfaces.
Limiting diffusion across grain boundaries maintains local chemical order.
Atomic diffusion controls rearrangements associated with chemical ordering, segregation, and decomposition in compositionally complex materials.
Kinetic hindrance from grain boundaries stabilizes structure and composition during high-temperature exposure.
Kinetic stabilization can complement or override thermodynamic stabilization from configurational entropy.
High-entropy alloys need not possess the ideal configurational entropy expected from completely random mixing because partial chemical order can reduce that entropy.
Nano-grained high-entropy alloys will exhibit delayed phase segregation relative to coarse-grained high-entropy alloys and lower-entropy alloys.
Nano-grained high-entropy alloys will exhibit less chemical inhomogeneity than the baseline alloys.
Nano-grained high-entropy alloys will exhibit postponed oxidation or ordering transitions relative to the baseline alloys.
Baseline alloys will begin degrading at lower temperatures or after fewer thermal cycles.
The prediction is bounded to grain sizes below approximately 100 nm and temperatures from 600°C to 1200°C.
Outside the stated grain-size and temperature bounds, oxidation kinetics or thermodynamic phase stability may dominate.
The relative quantitative contributions of kinetic barriers and configurational entropy may vary with composition and processing history.

Failure of the approximately 50 nm samples to show delayed transformations, reduced segregation, or lower diffusion rates relative to approximately 500 nm and lower-entropy controls would falsify the proposed primary grain-boundary mechanism.
